request: Let admins upload a CSV to bulk-create users.

labels.why: The commit rule determines which users appear in GET /users when a file contains both valid and invalid rows.
The upload response must let the admin locate a rejected row and understand what to correct.
Bulk creation needs a matching rule and a defined outcome for collisions with existing users and between rows in the upload.

labels.applies_part: Define which user fields the import may set and ensure an uploaded row cannot grant privileges.
labels.why: A field allowlist can enforce the privilege boundary here, while comparing assignable roles requires a role model absent from the user store.
The request reserves uploads for admins, so the upload endpoint needs its own enforceable authorization rule even though the server currently exposes only reads.
The importer needs a header contract to map columns to user fields and handle missing or unexpected columns.
Encoding, line endings and CSV quoting determine where headers, fields and records begin and end.

labels.applies_part: Specify whether users inserted from earlier rows remain in the store when a later row fails.
labels.why: Inserting a user changes observable state, while sending an invitation requires a mail capability absent from the program.
The HTTP handler needs an enforceable upload limit and a defined rejection outcome to bound the resources consumed by one request.
Empty input, a header with zero records and one data row are distinct boundary cases for the upload.
An admin can repeat a request after a lost response, so the specification must explain what happens to rows already created.
Processing after the HTTP request finishes and reporting later completion would add background jobs and a way to obtain their results.
Invitation volume and pacing belong to a mail service that neither the program nor the upload request calls for.

labels.applies_part: Define the initial record for each accepted row, including its ID, name, email and visibility through the existing reads.
labels.why: Creating the stored record is intrinsic to the import, while account activation, passwords and first sign-in require an account lifecycle the program lacks.

labels.applies_part: Specify where uploaded personal data is held during processing and when the raw file or any temporary copy is discarded.
labels.why: Handling and retention apply as soon as the server receives the bytes, while later download would require a retrievable file and a download endpoint.
The column contract can settle this by treating names and emails as text, defining how numeric IDs are assigned and excluding date or locale-based coercion.
Attributing a bulk write to its admin requires deciding what import details and timestamp to log without copying the raw personal data into the log.
Targeting an in-flight import for cancellation or a previous import for selective retry would add import controls beyond submitting a CSV.

labels.applies_part: Set and verify a processing-time bound for an upload at the supported size limit.
labels.why: Maximum-size performance belongs to the upload contract, while live progress would add a user-visible reporting channel.

labels.applies_part: Preserve existing user records and their behavior through the list and lookup endpoints when adding imported users.
labels.why: The store already serves existing records, while the server has no manual single-user creation path to preserve.

labels.applies_part: Bound field lengths and handle oversized or hostile values safely in the import and its HTTP result.
labels.why: Field validation applies to every upload, while formula execution on opening a result presupposes a spreadsheet-compatible export beyond the server's JSON responses.
